headline: Deer Island's Dawn Blitz: Blues and Bass Crash Bait Before the Ferries Run
subhead: The harbor islands are lighting up at first light while the North Shore ledges hold their pattern into the new moon.
body_markdown:
I made my call for this week Monday night looking at the tide chart: I'm staying inside the islands before sunrise, then running the boat up to Cape Ann in the evenings. That's where the action's been, and that's where I think it stays through the weekend.

Outside Deer Island, from about 4:30 to 8am, the harbor's been doing something I look forward to every summer — bait pods getting squeezed against the light and the edge of President Roads by the outgoing current, and blues and bass piling on top of them in full view. I've had mornings this week where I idled out of the marina in the dark, cut the engine off the Deer Island light, and watched the surface go white before I even had a lure tied on. Poppers and stickbaits worked over the boils — a Doc-style walker in bone or chartreuse, worked with a hard walk-the-dog cadence — and you don't need to be subtle about it. The blues are running 3 to 6 pounds and hitting like they're mad about something, and mixed in are schoolie-to-mid-20s bass that will occasionally give you a legitimate teeth-rattling take on a topwater plug. If you want the bigger bass specifically, switch over to a live mackerel under a balloon or slow-trolled on a stinger rig — that's been the ticket for the fish pushing 30-plus inches that are sitting a little deeper under the blitz, letting the blues do the dirty work up top.

This window is tide-dependent and it's tight. You want the last two hours of the outgoing pushing bait off the flats around Deer Island and Winthrop, and once the tide goes dead slack around mid-morning, the whole thing shuts off like someone flipped a switch. I've fished the same water at 11am with nothing to show for it. Get there early or don't bother.

Spectacle Island's north drop-off has been holding fish too, though it's a different program — this is a structure bite, not a blitz. I've been drifting live mackerel and chunked pogies along the 25 to 35-foot break on the last of the ebb, and picking up bass in the mid-20s to low 30s pretty consistently, along with a few bigger fish that came unglued before I could get a good look at them. The Graves, out past the outer islands, is worth a shot on a strong tide if you're comfortable running exposed water — that ledge has produced some of the better bass of the summer for guys fishing bucktails tipped with mackerel strips, worked slow along the bottom on the drift.

Nahant and Egg Rock have been steady on the North Shore side. Nothing explosive, but a reliable evening bite — eels and live mackerel fished tight to the rocks on the last two hours of the incoming, right at dusk. Cape Ann is the same story: Eastern Point and Bass Rocks are holding bass through the rock structure, and the pattern hasn't changed much since July. We said last week this holding pattern would carry through until water temps ease off in September, and that's exactly what's happening — no big shift, just steady work if you fish the tide right. What has changed is the tidal push building into the August 12 new moon, and I can already feel it sharpening the bite around current-driven spots like the Graves and the mouth of the harbor. Bigger swings mean more water moving, more bait getting displaced, and more fish committing to structure instead of scattering.

Flounder guys, don't sleep on Duxbury Bay and Kingston Bay right now. The flats are holding decent numbers on the last of the ebb tide, sandworms and clam strips on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished slow along the mud-to-sand transitions. Plymouth Harbor's been quieter but not dead — a few keeper flounder came off the flats on calm mornings before the wind picked up.

Cod and haddock guys are going to want to keep an eye offshore. There's real bluefin interest building out toward Stellwagen Bank right now on green water and bait concentrations — we flagged that trend last week and it's holding. It's not squarely my inshore program, but if you're running a bigger boat out of Gloucester and have the range, that's worth knowing about before you commit a whole day to bottom fishing.

Looking ahead, I expect the harbor blitz to hold through the weekend as long as bait stays stacked against Deer Island — and with the new moon building, I think it actually gets better before it tapers. The North Shore rock bite should stay steady through the ledges at Nahant and Cape Ann, no reason to expect a shift there yet. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be off Deer Island at 4:30, poppers rigged, watching the light for the first boil. If the harbor's dead by the time you get there, Spectacle Island's drop-off is my backup, and it rarely lets me down on a clean outgoing tide.
